Abstract
Highlights
What are the main findings?
The paper frames AI-enabled sensing as a human–cyberspace relation rather than only a signal-processing pipeline.
Three sub-domains are proposed: exteroceptive, interoceptive, and machine-native cyber-sensing, with an integrated crosswalk showing their distinct evaluation burdens.
What are the implications of the main findings?
AI-sensor evaluation should pair technical metrics with appropriately operationalized human-centered measures of perceptual coherence, interoceptive agency, and perceptual explainability.
The Cyberism framework gives intelligent-sensor research a design agenda that links edge AI sensing with human autonomy, oversight, and equity in cyber-mediated sensing.
Abstract
Artificial intelligence (AI) and sensing technologies increasingly mediate how humans encounter physical, bodily, and digital environments. Yet intelligent-sensor frameworks still emphasize accuracy, latency, power, and robustness while giving less attention to the perceptual relation created between humans and cyberspace. This conceptual and integrative review uses directed conceptual synthesis, purposive literature selection, contrastive case analysis, and negative-case testing to develop the perception–interaction layer of Cyberism for AI-enabled sensing. 4. Discussion
4.1. From Accuracy Optimization to Perceptual Experience Design
The first implication of the Cyberism perception–interaction layer is a shift from accuracy optimization to perceptual experience design. Accuracy remains essential, but it is not sufficient. Accuracy measures the gap between a system output and a physical or labeled reference. Perceptual experience design asks a different question: whether the user can integrate the sensed and inferred information into action, trust, and self-understanding. Automation research shows that technically capable systems can still produce misuse, disuse, or inappropriate reliance when human understanding and trust are poorly calibrated [

4.10. Limitations
This paper has limitations. First, it proposes a conceptual framework and a validation protocol but reports no empirical validation. The categories of exteroceptive, interoceptive, and machine-native cyber-sensing should be tested across more domains, including environmental sensing, industrial inspection, smart homes, affective computing, and assistive technologies. Second, the literature synthesis is purposive rather than systematic, and the case studies are illustrative rather than exhaustive; neither supports prevalence estimates or claims of comprehensive coverage. Third, the framework is intentionally human-centered, which means it may require extension for ecosystems in which nonhuman agents, robots, or distributed infrastructures are the primary users of sensing outputs. Fourth, Cyberism is itself an emerging doctrine; its terminology, construct measures, and boundaries will need refinement through use by sensor engineers, HCI researchers, clinicians, ethicists, and social scientists. 5. Conclusions
AI-enabled sensing is becoming a primary interface between humans and cyberspace. This article introduced the perception–interaction layer of Cyberism as a framework for understanding and designing that interface. The central argument is simple: intelligent sensors should be evaluated not only by what they measure, but also by what perceptual relation they create.
The paper identified three sub-domains. Exteroceptive cyber-sensing extends and reconstructs external senses; interoceptive cyber-sensing externalizes and interprets internal bodily states; and machine-native cyber-sensing translates nonhuman modalities into humanly actionable perception. These sub-domains clarify why haptic feedback, wearable health sensing, and autonomous driving perception raise different human–cyberspace questions even when all are technically AI sensor systems.
The proposed three-level methodological agenda links engineering design, empirical human study, and philosophical reflection.
